query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Toughness retention in high-entropy alloys under demanding conditions is governed predominantly by the stabilization of grain boundaries through solute segregation. A tailored heat treatment that enhances this segregation will modify the grain boundary structure—in particular, promoting a serrated morphology—that in turn leads to more uniform strain distribution and improved crack deflection, thereby retaining higher toughness compared to conventional processing.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy produced in the as-cast or standard heat-treated state with typical grain boundary composition and morphology.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored heat treatment/annealing protocol with controlled cooling designed to promote selective solute segregation at grain boundaries (without altering the primary bulk phase) to enhance grain boundary stability and produce a serrated morphology.
generation.conditions: Extreme mechanical and thermal loading conditions (e.g., high strain rates and elevated temperatures) that are representative of demanding engineering applications, while ensuring processing temperatures remain below thresholds that induce wholesale phase transformations.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary structure and chemistry—specifically, the degree of solute segregation that leads to stabilized, serrated grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced grain boundary stability via solute segregation reduces local strain concentrations and facilitates crack deflection and bridging. This mitigates intergranular crack initiation and propagation during high-load conditions, resulting in retained overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventionally processed samples, specimens receiving the tailored heat treatment will exhibit higher fracture toughness, delayed crack initiation, and increased ductility, with microstructural analyses (via SEM/TEM) revealing a more serrated and stable grain boundary morphology that correlates with improved crack deflection.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy specimens processed with standard cooling and heat treatment protocols that do not specifically target grain boundary stabilization.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys with single-phase or controlled multiphase structures where the bulk microstructure is maintained, and the processing temperatures are kept below levels that trigger extensive recrystallization or phase transformation.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contribution of grain boundary stabilization versus other mechanisms (such as dislocation mobility or phase transformation kinetics) to overall toughness retention remains partially uncertain and may vary with the specific alloy composition and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens: one set is subjected to the tailored heat treatment aimed at enhancing grain boundary stabilization (via controlled solute segregation), while the other set undergoes a conventional heat treatment. Both sets are then exposed to identical extreme mechanical and thermal loading conditions. In situ microscopy (such as SEM or TEM) is employed to monitor grain boundary morphology and crack propagation behavior.
measurements: Grain boundary morphology and serration (via SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored heat-treated specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in fracture toughness, ductility, or evidence of enhanced crack deflection (as indicated by comparable or inferior measurements to the baseline material), then the hypothesis—that grain boundary stabilization via solute segregation governs toughness retention—will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Despite the extremely high hardness of recently proposed high-entropy carbides (HECs), the low fracture toughness limits their applications in harsh mechanical environment. Here, we introduce a metastability engineering strategy to achieve superhard HECs with enhanced toughness via in-situ metastable particles. This is realized by developing a (WTaNbZrTi)C HEC showing a solid solution matrix with uniformly dispersed in-situ tetragonal and monoclinic ZrO2 particles. Apart from a high hardness of 21.0 GPa, the HEC can obtain an enhanced fracture toughness of 5.89 MPa·m1/2, significantly exceeding the value predicted by rule of mixture and that of other reported HECs. The toughening effect is primarily attributed to the transformation of the metastable tetragonal ZrO2 particles under mechanical loading, which promotes crack tip shielding mechanisms including crack deflection, crack bridging and crack branching. The work demonstrates the concept of using in-situ metastable particles for toughening bulk high-entropy ceramics by taking advantage of their compositional flexibility. The complex impedance spectra of the CTO-based ceramics were measured at 500 °C and were fitted according to the equivalent circuit,, which reflects the electrical response from grains and grain boundaries, respectively (Fig. 2a). The spectra for all samples consist of one obvious arc attributed to the grain boundary response, while that of grains is indistinguishable due to their relatively small resistance. The arc diameter gradually decreased as more elements were introduced into the A-site of CTO, indicating a reducing trend of grain boundary resistance, which can be attributed to larger amounts of defects aggregated at the grain boundaries (Fig. S4).

AbstractMulti‐principal element alloys (MPEA) demonstrate exceptional stability during rapid solidification, making them ideal candidates for additive manufacturing and other high‐design‐flexibility techniques. Unexpectedly, MPEA failure often mimics that of conventional metals, with strain localization along phase or grain boundaries leading to typical crack initiation. Most strategies aim at reducing strain localization either suppress the formation of high‐energy sites or dissipate energy at crack tips to enhance toughness, rarely achieving a synergy of both. Inspired by the microstructure of mouse enamel, nanoscale body‐centered cubic (BCC) and face‐centered cubic (FCC) phases into MPEAs are introduced, stabilized at phase boundaries to provide ample plastic space for dislocation‐mediated deformation. This approach overcomes the local hardening limitations of nanoscale alloys and harmonizes traditional toughening mechanisms—such as crack deflection, blocking, and bridging—to mitigate strain localization. From a mechanical perspective, the ideal strain concentration resistance strategy is to suppress the generation of strain concentration sites and dissipate the strain energy at the crack tip. However, the microstructures that affect these two stages seem to be in a contradictory state. More specifically, in NG/UFG high‐strength alloys, the limited diffusion and interaction of dislocations within a small volume inhibit the continuous nucleation of new dislocations and the sustained activation of displacement deformation mechanisms.[ ,  ] Under external load, deformation is regulated by grain boundary sliding and separation to accommodate the mutual compression of adjacent fine grains.[  ] Dislocation mechanism‐driven intragranular plasticity becomes more difficult, but this leads to a small space passivation crack propagation mechanism, and this strength enhancement is usually due to geometric space constraints at the expense of macro/micro local damage resistance and plastic stability.

The novelty of this work lies in the systematic investigation of densification behavior, microstructural evolution, and mechanical properties of atomized Cantor alloy powders consolidated by spark plasma sintering under varied temperature and dwell time conditions. This study reveals a non-linear relationship between sintering temperature and relative density, and notably documents grain growth during the ultrafast SPS process, challenging the common assumption that SPS inherently suppresses grain coarsening. Additionally, the retention of a homogeneous single-phase FCC structure without phase segregation, paired with enhanced mechanical strength, emphasizes the strong interplay between sintering kinetics and microstructural stability, which has significant implications for the processing of high-entropy alloys.

Different from the saturation magnetization, the coercivity is expected to be sensitive to the grain size, impurity, deformation, and the subsequent heat-treatment process. Specifically, the various microstructures, together with the lattice distortion induced by Al and Si, will inevitably affect the magnetic domain-wall movement and, thus, the coercivity. This effect is the most obvious when x equals 0.3, at which BCC and FCC phases coexist (Figure 4), and the phase boundaries may greatly hinder the domain-wall shift, resulting in the highest coercivity. In alloys of a single-phase structure, such as A4 and A5, the grain size may also matter. For example, the A5 alloy has larger grains than the A4 alloy, such that the domain-wall movement of the A5 alloy is likely to be easier than the A4 alloy, which explains the lower coecivity of the A5 alloy than the A4 alloy. Since Hc is so sensitive to the microstructure, it is likely that at a given composition (and thus Ms), the coercivity can be tuned within a fairly-wide range by, for example, the quenching-rate control and heat/pressure treatment. This feature provides opportunities to further reduce the Hc of our alloys.

The so-called “high entropy alloys” (HEAs) are a class of emergent transition metal alloys that hold great potential for advanced manufacturing, and which may impact magnetocalorics. These are near equimolar alloys with high entropy of mixing when in a random solid solution. These materials have been pursued for high hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, which are attractive properties for a myriad of applications. Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx is an example HEA system with tunable magnetic properties. The addition of Pd was shown to change the critical temperature (Tc) from 300 to 500 K for x = 1 to 2, along with enhancement of the saturation magnetization; previous works have used high percentages of Pd as a stabilizing agent in similar high strength bulk alloys. In this work, we explore the magnetic properties of the Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloy family, as-rolled and after annealing, with low molar fractions of Pd. We find improvement in the magnetocaloric properties throughout the system. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior suggest this originates predominately from the homogenization of the alloy with both Pd and heat treatment. decision.trend: Early high‐entropy alloy research focused on broad alloy compositional adjustments and empirical correlations that indirectly linked microstructural evolution to toughness. A breakthrough came with in situ TEM studies (PMC4682111), where nanoscale processes such as the motion of partial dislocations, stacking fault formation, and the formation of nanotwin bridges were directly visualized and linked to damage tolerance. Subsequent work (PMC5893566) expanded on this by considering phase transformation effects – showing that a switch between fcc and hcp phases, triggered by dislocation slip and boundary interactions, can modulate mechanical properties – while later atomistic and bicrystal studies (PMC7801446) probed the role of grain boundaries as nucleation sites for deformation features. Despite these advances, no study has isolated a single governing microstructural mechanism responsible for toughness retention versus loss under extreme conditions.
decision.unsolved: The outstanding challenge is to definitively identify which microstructural process—be it grain boundary cohesion/stability, phase transformation kinetics, or dislocation-mediated mechanisms—dominantly governs the retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys under demanding conditions. In particular, isolating a controlled change that singles out one of these variables while decoupling its effects from the others remains unaddressed.
decision.lever: Implement a tailored heat treatment/annealing protocol to systematically vary grain boundary composition/stability (for example, by controllably promoting or suppressing solute segregation without altering the bulk phase)
decision.why: This approach directly follows from the trend where in situ and simulation studies highlighted the importance of grain boundary‐mediated processes in toughness retention (e.g., nanoscale crack bridging and dislocation nucleation at boundaries). By deliberately controlling the grain boundary state via heat treatment, one can test if enhanced boundary stability leads to increased resistance to toughness degradation relative to a baseline condition. Observing improved crack deflection and delayed failure would support the hypothesis, whereas an absence of these changes would falsify it.
